title: The Night J.P. Morgan Locked Bankers In His Library To Stop The Panic Of 1907
sources: The Morgan Library & Museum, 'Panic of 1907' (Morgan summoned trust presidents to his library and locked the doors)

Federal Reserve History / Boston Fed 'Panic of 1907' (United Copper corner, Knickerbocker run 22 Oct, Trust Company of America, $23.6M pledged by 14 banks on 24 Oct, Cortelyou ~$25M, TC&I purchase, Aldrich-Vreeland Act, National Monetary Commission)
Bruner & Carr, The Panic of 1907 (excerpt via NPR): 4:45 a.m. signatures, $25M trust pool; Edward King of Union Trust
Library of Congress Inside Adams blog: United Copper and the Panic of 1907
Pujo Committee testimony, Dec 1912 ('the first thing is character'); Federal Reserve Act signed 23 Dec 1913
Footage/photos: Library of Congress, Wikimedia Commons (public domain pre-1928 images); early New York films (Edison/Biograph, public domain)

Hedged in script: 'this is the place to stop the trouble' (usual telling); locked-door attempt to leave + key in pocket (one account); 'here's the place, King' (one account); cheering on the floor (it was said); copper price ~$60 -> ~$10; ~$8M paid out; ~$30M city bonds

beats.text: New York. A Saturday night in November 1907. Snow-cold air on Madison Avenue.
Inside a marble library, the most powerful bankers in America are waiting.
In the next room, a seventy-year-old man is playing cards by himself.

v.q: J. P. Morgan West Room study

beats.text: His name is John Pierpont Morgan, and tonight he holds the country's money system in his hands.
The bankers think they can go home whenever they like. They are wrong. The front door has been locked.
This is the story of how one banker stopped a crash with a locked door, and why America decided no one man should ever do that again.
To see why that door mattered, go back four weeks. It starts with a bet on copper.
In October 1907, a mining millionaire named Augustus Heinze and his brother Otto tried to corner the shares of their own company, United Copper.
The plan was simple. Buy up the shares, squeeze the traders who had bet against them, and force the price up.
For one day it worked. Then the traders found shares somewhere else, and the price collapsed.
In a few days the stock fell from around sixty dollars to around ten.
A copper deal gone wrong should have been a small story. But the Heinze brothers were tied to banks.
And in 1907 there was no central bank. No Federal Reserve. No lender of last resort.
If people panicked and wanted their cash back, nobody had to save them.
The fear jumped from copper to the trust companies. These were lightly regulated banks that paid high interest and kept little cash.
The third biggest in New York was the Knickerbocker Trust, a marble temple on Fifth Avenue.
Its president, Charles Barney, had business links to the men behind the copper corner.
On the twenty-first of October, a big bank said it would no longer clear the Knickerbocker's cheques. The news was out by morning.
Morgan had just come back from a church meeting in Virginia. His men studied the Knickerbocker's books through the night.
Their answer was cold. They could not be sure the Knickerbocker was solid. Morgan decided not to save it.
On the twenty-second of October, the line outside the Knickerbocker stretched down the street.
Clerks paid out about eight million dollars in less than three hours. Then, around noon, the doors closed.
Charles Barney never recovered. He died a few weeks later.
Now every depositor in New York asked the same question. Is my bank next?
The next target was the Trust Company of America. People lined up before dawn.
Morgan sent a young banker named Benjamin Strong to check its books. Strong reported it was in trouble, but basically sound.
By the usual telling, Morgan said: this, then, is the place to stop the trouble.

v.text: This is the place to stop the trouble.

beats.text: Cash was carried in through the crowds. The Trust Company of America survived the day.
Washington moved too. Treasury Secretary George Cortelyou came to New York and put about twenty-five million dollars of government money into the banks.
But the government was not running the rescue. Morgan was.
On the twenty-fourth of October, the president of the Stock Exchange walked across the street to Morgan's office.
Brokers could not borrow money at any price. The interest rate on overnight loans had shot up to one hundred percent.

v.q: New York Stock Exchange trading floor 1900s

beats.text: He said the Exchange might have to close early. Morgan told him it would not close.
Morgan called the bank presidents into his office. Within minutes they pledged more than twenty-three million dollars.

v.q: J.P. Morgan and Co. building Wall Street

beats.text: When the money reached the trading floor, it was said the brokers' cheering could be heard outside.
Days later, the City of New York itself was running short. Morgan's group agreed to buy about thirty million dollars of city bonds.
On Sunday, churches across the city were asked to preach calm from the pulpit.
Each day, Morgan stopped one fire. And each night, a new one started.
By the first week of November, two fires were burning at once.
Fire one: the trust companies were still bleeding cash, and the strong ones refused to help the weak ones.
Fire two: a big brokerage firm, Moore and Schley, was about to fail.
Its loans were backed by shares in a southern steel company, Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad.

v.q: Tennessee Coal Iron and Railroad Company

beats.text: If that firm went down, the whole market could go with it.
So on Saturday, the second of November, Morgan called everyone to his private library on Thirty-Sixth Street.
The trust company presidents sat in one room. Morgan's own bankers sat in another.
Morgan sat alone in his study, under his paintings, playing patience with a deck of cards.
Hours passed. Midnight passed. The trust presidents argued and would not agree.
Then, by one account, some of them decided to leave. They found the front door locked. The key was in Morgan's pocket.
Morgan's demand was simple. The trust companies would raise twenty-five million dollars together to protect the weaker ones.
Around a quarter to five in the morning, Morgan walked in with a paper and a pen.
By one account, he handed the pen to Edward King, the leader of the trust presidents, and said: here's the place, King.
King signed. The others followed. Then the door was opened.
That still left fire two. Morgan's answer was to have U.S. Steel buy the Tennessee company, so the brokerage firm's shares would be worth something again.
There was one problem. U.S. Steel was already huge, and President Theodore Roosevelt was attacking big trusts.
So two U.S. Steel men, Henry Clay Frick and Elbert Gary, took a night train to Washington.
On Monday morning, before the market opened, they saw Roosevelt at the White House.
Roosevelt said he would not object. The deal went through, and the market held.
Critics later said Morgan's company got a rich prize very cheaply in the middle of a panic. The government's later antitrust case against U.S. Steel raised that deal again.
The panic ended. Morgan was called the man who saved Wall Street.
But the same story frightened a lot of people. One private banker had just decided which banks lived and which banks died.
The Knickerbocker was allowed to fall. The Trust Company of America was saved. Morgan made that call in his own offices.
And Morgan was seventy. What would happen in the next panic, when he was gone?
In 1908, Congress passed an emergency currency law and set up a National Monetary Commission to study the problem.
In 1910, a few senators and bankers met in secret at Jekyll Island in Georgia to draft a plan.
In 1912, Morgan was called before Congress. Asked if credit was based on money or property, he answered: the first thing is character.
He died in Rome in March 1913.
Nine months later, President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act.

v.q: Woodrow Wilson signing Federal Reserve Act

beats.text: From then on, the job Morgan did that night would belong to a public central bank, not a private man with a key.
So who won the Panic of 1907? The Heinze brothers lost their corner. Barney lost everything. The Knickerbocker lost its doors.
Morgan won the week, and U.S. Steel won a steel company.
But in the long run, the real winner was the idea that the system should never again depend on one man.
Morgan stopped the crash by locking the door. America answered by building a bank that would not need him.
If you like true business wars from the history books, subscribe. Next time, it's another boardroom where someone does not get to leave.
